newsitem.title: USA: Latam activity dominates U.S. foreign crude scene.
newsitem.headline: Latam activity dominates U.S. foreign crude scene.

text.p: Latin American activity dominated the foreign crude scene in the U.S. Gulf Coast on Wednesday amid a continued tight trans-Atlantic arbitrage, traders said.
Trading was subdued, with many players attending a BP-sponsored event in Cleveland, Ohio.
"It's very quiet. Western Hemisphere crudes seem to be mostly all placed for July," an East Coast trader said.
Topping the day's events were two crude tankers held up in the Colombian port of Covenas where they were unable to load as a result of back-to-back rebel bombings of the Cano Limon-Covenas pipeline.
Despite the delay, Colombia's state oil company Ecopetrol had not declared force majeur on its crude contracts.
Although pipeline bombings are frequent in Colombia, the two recent blasts left little volume in the two million barrel floating storage unit at Covenas.
The pipeline is expected to be repaired sometime between Thursday and the weekend, allowing the tankers to load their respective cargoes.

One tanker, a Panamax vessel named Santa Panaglia, was supposed to load around 400,000 barrels of Cano Limon crude on Tuesday. The tanker was bound for Peru for Spain's Repsol, which controls the La Pampilla refinery.
The other tanker, named Harrier, is believed to belong to Shell, although this information could not be immediately confirmed.
Elsewhere in the region, a group of Argentine producers was accepting bids on Thursday for 30,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Escalante crude, either on a term or spot basis, trade sources said.
On Tuesday, an equity producer sold a cargo of Cusiana crude loading July 30 to August 1 to a U.S. major for $1.29 under September West Texas Intermediate/Cushing.
Also on Tuesday, a U.S. major bought a cargo of Ecuadoran Oriente crude for end-July delivery to the East Coast for $2.86 under September WTI/Cushing.
State oil company Petroecuador recently raised its formula price for Oriente by 30 cents a barrel, retroactive to June 1.
Meanwhile, North Sea and West African offerings were scarce, reflecting a continued narrow arbitrage.
The spread between August WTI and Brent was around $1.15-25 a barrel late on Wednesday.
